row.questionText: Prove that √3 is irrational.
solutionSteps: Assume √3 is rational, so √3 = p/q where p, q are co-prime integers, q ≠ 0.; Squaring: 3 = p²/q², so p² = 3q². [1]
This means 3 divides p², hence 3 divides p. Let p = 3m.; Then 9m² = 3q², so q² = 3m², meaning 3 divides q² and hence 3 divides q. [1]
But p and q were co-prime, contradiction. Hence √3 is irrational. [1]

Both p and q divisible by 3 contradicts gcd(p, q) = 1.
Hence √3 is irrational.

row.questionText: Prove that √3 is irrational.
row.answer: Assume, to the contrary, that √3 is rational. Then √3 = a/b for coprime integers a, b with b ≠ 0. Squaring: 3 = a²/b², so a² = 3b². Hence 3 divides a², and by Theorem 1.3 (prime p | a² ⇒ p | a), 3 divides a. Write a = 3c. Then (3c)² = 3b² ⇒ 9c² = 3b² ⇒ b² = 3c². So 3 divides b², hence 3 divides b. Thus 3 is a common factor of a and b, contradicting the assumption that a and b are coprime. Hence √3 is irrational.
solutionSteps: Suppose √3 is rational. Then √3 = a/b with gcd(a, b) = 1 and b ≠ 0.
Squaring: 3 = a²/b² ⇒ a² = 3b² ⇒ 3 | a².
By the prime-divides-square theorem, 3 | a. Write a = 3c.
Substitute: 9c² = 3b² ⇒ b² = 3c². So 3 | b², hence 3 | b.
Now 3 | a and 3 | b, contradicting gcd(a, b) = 1. Hence √3 is irrational.
row.strategyHint: Same template as √2 proof; replace 2 with 3.

row.questionText: Prove that √2 is irrational.
solutionSteps: Assume √2 is rational. Then √2 = p/q where p and q are coprime integers with q ≠ 0.
Squaring both sides: 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q².
Since 2 divides p², and 2 is prime, 2 divides p (by the prime divisibility lemma).
Let p = 2k for some integer k. Then p² = 4k².
Substituting: 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k².
Since 2 divides q², and 2 is prime, 2 divides q.
Now 2 divides both p and q, contradicting gcd(p, q) = 1.
Hence our assumption is false. Therefore, √2 is irrational.

row.questionText: Prove that √2 is irrational.
row.answer: We use the method of proof by contradiction. Assume, to the contrary, that √2 is rational. Then √2 = a/b for some coprime integers a, b with b ≠ 0. Squaring: 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b². Hence 2 divides a², which (by the theorem 'if a prime p divides a², then p divides a') implies 2 divides a. Write a = 2c. Substituting: (2c)² = 2b² ⇒ 4c² = 2b² ⇒ b² = 2c². So 2 divides b² and hence 2 divides b. But then 2 is a common factor of a and b, which contradicts our assumption that a and b are coprime. The contradiction arose from supposing √2 rational. Therefore √2 is irrational.
solutionSteps: Assume √2 is rational. Then √2 = a/b for some integers a, b coprime, b ≠ 0.
Square both sides: 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b². Hence 2 | a².
By Theorem 1.3 (if prime p | a², then p | a), we get 2 | a. Write a = 2c for some integer c.
Substitute: (2c)² = 2b² ⇒ 4c² = 2b² ⇒ b² = 2c². So 2 | b², which gives 2 | b.
Thus 2 divides BOTH a and b, contradicting gcd(a, b) = 1. The assumption is false; hence √2 is irrational.
row.strategyHint: Standard four-step contradiction: assume rational → derive 2 | a → derive 2 | b → contradict coprimality.

row.questionText: A train travels 360 km at a uniform speed. If the speed had been 5 km/h more, it would have taken 1 hour less for the same journey. Find the speed of the train.
row.answer: The original speed of the train is 40 km/h.
solutionSteps: Let the original speed be x km/h (x > 0).
Time taken at speed x = 360/x hours; time at increased speed (x + 5) = 360/(x + 5) hours.
Given difference of 1 hour: 360/x − 360/(x + 5) = 1.
Reject x = −45 (speed positive). Hence original speed = 40 km/h. Verify: 360/40 − 360/45 = 9 − 8 = 1 ✓
row.strategyHint: Distance / time pattern: form an equation in time difference (or sum); apply the quadratic formula.

solutionSteps: Let speed = x km/h. Time = 360/x hours.; New speed = (x+5) km/h. New time = 360/(x+5) hours. [1]
Using quadratic formula or factoring: x = (−5 ± √(25+7200))/2 = (−5 ± √7225)/2 = (−5 ± 85)/2.; x = 80/2 = 40 (taking positive value). Speed = 40 km/h. [1]
Verify: Time = 360/40 = 9 h. At 45 km/h: 360/45 = 8 h. Difference = 1 h. ✓ [1]
row.answer: The speed of the train is 40 km/h.

row.questionText: Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
solutionSteps: Construction: Draw a circle with centre O and mark the point of tangency. Draw the tangent line at that point.; Let ABCD be a parallelogram circumscribing the circle; AP = AS, BP = BQ, CR = CQ, DR = DS (tangent lengths) [1]
AB = AP + PB, CD = CR + RD; BC = BQ + QC, AD = AS + SD; AB + CD = AP + PB + CR + RD [1]
BC + AD = BQ + QC + AS + SD; Since opposite sides of parallelogram are equal: AB = CD, BC = AD; 2AB = (AP+AS) + (PB+QC) + ... → all sides equal → rhombus [1]
row.finalAnswer: Proved: all sides are equal → rhombus

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
solutionSteps: Let ABCD be a parallelogram circumscribing a circle, touching AB, BC, CD, DA at P, Q, R, S.
By equal tangents: AP = AS, BP = BQ, CQ = CR, DR = DS.
AB + CD = (AP + PB) + (CR + RD) = (AS + SD) + (BQ + QC) = AD + BC.
Since ABCD is a parallelogram, AB = CD and AD = BC. So 2AB = 2AD ⇒ AB = AD.
Hence all sides AB = BC = CD = DA, i.e., ABCD is a rhombus.
row.finalAnswer: Proved: a parallelogram that circumscribes a circle is a rhombus.

row.questionText: Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
row.answer: The parallelogram is a rhombus (all sides equal, proved)
solutionSteps: GIVEN: ABCD is a parallelogram that circumscribes a circle. The circle touches AB at P, BC at Q, CD at R and DA at S.
TO PROVE: AB = BC = CD = DA  (i.e., ABCD is a rhombus)
PROOF: Since tangents from an external point are equal:
From A: AP = AS  ...(i)
From B: BP = BQ  ...(ii)
From C: CQ = CR  ...(iii)
From D: DR = DS  ...(iv)
Adding (i) + (ii) + (iii) + (iv):
AP + BP + CQ + DR = AS + BQ + CR + DS
(AP + BP) + (CQ + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CR)
AB + CD = AD + BC  ...(v)
Since ABCD is a parallelogram: AB = CD and AD = BC  ...(vi)
Substituting (vi) in (v):
AB + AB = AD + AD
2AB = 2AD
AB = AD
Since AB = CD and AD = BC and AB = AD:
AB = BC = CD = DA
Therefore ABCD is a rhombus. Hence Proved.
row.finalAnswer: ABCD is a rhombus (AB = BC = CD = DA proved)
row.explanation: Apply equal tangent lengths from all four vertices to get AB+CD = AD+BC. For a parallelogram AB=CD and AD=BC. Substituting gives 2AB = 2AD, so AB = AD, making all sides equal.

Let the circle touch AB, BC, CD, DA at P, Q, R, S. Tangents from an external point are equal: AP = AS = a, BP = BQ = b, CQ = CR = c, DR = DS = d [½]
AB + CD = (a+b) + (c+d); AD + BC = (a+d) + (b+c) [½]
Both equal a + b + c + d, hence AB + CD = AD + BC [1]

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: A quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle. Prove that AB + CD = AD + BC.
solutionSteps: GIVEN: Quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle. The circle touches AB at P, BC at Q, CD at R and DA at S.
TO PROVE: AB + CD = AD + BC
PROOF: Since tangents from an external point to a circle are equal in length:
From vertex A: AP = AS  ...(i)
From vertex B: BP = BQ  ...(ii)
From vertex C: CQ = CR  ...(iii)
From vertex D: DR = DS  ...(iv)
Adding all four equations (i) + (ii) + (iii) + (iv):
AP + BP + CQ + DR = AS + BQ + CR + DS
Grouping the left side:
(AP + BP) + (CQ + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CR)
AB + CD = AD + BC   [since AP+BP = AB, CQ+DR = CD, AS+DS = AD, BQ+CR = BC]
Hence Proved.
row.finalAnswer: AB + CD = AD + BC (proved using equal tangent lengths from each vertex)
row.explanation: The circle touches each side at one point. From each vertex, two equal tangents are drawn. Sum the four pairs, group by sides to get AB + CD = AD + BC.
row.strategyHint: Label the four tangent points P, Q, R, S on sides AB, BC, CD, DA. Apply equal tangents from each of the four vertices. Sum all four equations and regroup.

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ.
solutionSteps: GIVEN: Circle with centre O. TP and TQ are tangents from external point T touching circle at P and Q.
TO PROVE: ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ
PROOF: Since tangents from external point are equal: TP = TQ  ...(i)
Therefore △TPQ is isosceles.
∠TPQ = ∠TQP  (base angles of isosceles △TPQ)  ...(ii)
Let ∠TPQ = ∠TQP = x
In △TPQ: ∠PTQ + ∠TPQ + ∠TQP = 180°
Now, TP is a tangent and OP is the radius at P.
∠OPT = 90°  (tangent ⊥ radius)  ...(iv)
∠OPQ = ∠OPT − ∠TPQ = 90° − x  ...(v)
Therefore 2∠OPQ = 2(90° − x) = 180° − 2x  ...(vi)
From (iii) and (vi):
∠PTQ = 180° − 2x = 2∠OPQ. Hence Proved.
row.explanation: TP = TQ (equal tangents) makes △TPQ isosceles. Let base angles = x. ∠PTQ = 180°−2x. Since ∠OPT = 90°, ∠OPQ = 90°−x. So 2∠OPQ = 180°−2x = ∠PTQ.
row.strategyHint: Use TP = TQ (isosceles triangle). Let base angle = x. Express ∠PTQ in terms of x. Use ∠OPT = 90° to express ∠OPQ in terms of x. Show they match.

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.
solutionSteps: Let ∠PTQ = θ. Tangents from external point: TP = TQ ⟹ ΔTPQ is isosceles. So ∠TPQ = ∠TQP = (180° − θ)/2 = 90° − θ/2.
OP ⊥ PT (tangent ⊥ radius) ⟹ ∠OPT = 90°.
∠OPQ = ∠OPT − ∠TPQ = 90° − (90° − θ/2) = θ/2 = ½ × ∠PTQ. Hence ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.

solutionSteps: Let the circle touch AB at F and AC at E. Then BD = BF = 8, DC = CE = 6, and let AF = AE = x.
Area of ∆ABC by Heron-like decomposition using incircle: Area = r × s where s = semi-perimeter.
Compute area another way using ∆OBC, ∆OCA, ∆OAB each with height = r = 4: Area = (1/2)×4×(BC + CA + AB) = 2 × 2s = 4s? Actually Area = r·s.
Also Area² = s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c) where a = BC = 14, b = CA = 6 + x, c = AB = 8 + x. s = 14 + x.
(rs)² = s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c) ⇒ r²s = (s − a)(s − b)(s − c).
AB = 8 + 7 = 15 cm and AC = 6 + 7 = 13 cm.

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
solutionSteps: Construction: Draw a circle with centre O and point P on the circle. Draw the tangent l at P and radius OP. Assume l is not perpendicular to OP and derive a contradiction.; Let O be centre, P be point on circle, line l be tangent at P [1]
Assume l is not ⊥ to OP. Draw OQ ⊥ l where Q is on l; Then OQ < OP (perpendicular is shortest distance) [1]
But Q is on tangent l, and l touches circle only at P; So Q must be outside the circle → OQ > OP (radius) [1]
This contradicts OQ < OP [1]
Hence our assumption is wrong, l ⊥ OP [1]

row.questionText: Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
row.answer: The tangent at a point on a circle is perpendicular to the radius through that point.
row.finalAnswer: If OP is radius and PT is tangent at P, then OP ⟂ PT.
row.explanation: Join the centre O to the point of contact P. Any other point Q on the tangent has OQ > OP, so OP is the shortest distance from O to the tangent. Hence OP ⟂ tangent at P.
solutionSteps: Consider circle with centre O and tangent at P touching circle.; Join OP and any other segment OQ to a point Q on the tangent. [½]
Use the property that the shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular.; Show that OP is the shortest distance. [½]
Conclude that OP ⟂ tangent at P. [1]
row.strategyHint: Think of shortest distance from a point to a line being the perpendicular segment.

row.subject: Science
row.questionText: Why do we apply paint on iron articles?
row.answer: Paint forms a protective coating that prevents iron from coming in contact with air (oxygen) and moisture. This prevents the oxidation of iron, i.e. rusting (corrosion).
solutionSteps: [0.5 mark] Rusting of iron requires both air (oxygen) and moisture.
[0.5 mark] Paint creates a barrier that prevents these reactants from reaching the iron surface.
[0.5 mark] Without contact between iron and O₂/H₂O, rusting cannot occur.
[0.5 mark] Hence painting prevents corrosion and prolongs the life of the iron article.
row.finalAnswer: To prevent rusting by blocking contact between iron and air/moisture.

row.subject: Science
row.questionText: What is hydrogenation? What is its industrial application?
row.answer: Hydrogenation is the addition of H₂ to an unsaturated hydrocarbon (containing C=C or C≡C) in the presence of a catalyst (usually Ni). E.g., R-CH=CH-R' + H₂ --(Ni)--> R-CH₂-CH₂-R'. Industrial application: hydrogenation of vegetable oils (which contain unsaturated fatty acids) to form solid fats like vanaspati ghee.
solutionSteps: Hydrogenation: addition of H₂ across C=C or C≡C, catalysed by Ni (or Pt/Pd).
Reaction: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃.
Industrial use: vegetable oils + H₂ (Ni catalyst) → solid fat (vanaspati / hydrogenated oil).
row.finalAnswer: Addition of H₂ to unsaturated compound (Ni catalyst). Used to make vanaspati from oils.

row.subject: Science
row.questionText: What happens at the synapse between two neurons?
row.answer: At the synapse (gap between two neurons), the electrical impulse arriving at the axonal end of the first neuron triggers the release of chemicals (neurotransmitters). These chemicals diffuse across the synapse and generate a new electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron.
solutionSteps: Electrical impulse reaches the axonal end of pre-synaptic neuron.
It triggers release of chemicals (neurotransmitters) into the synaptic gap.
Chemicals diffuse across the synapse and bind to receptors on the dendrite of the next neuron.
A new electrical impulse is generated in the post-synaptic neuron.
row.finalAnswer: Electrical → chemical → electrical signal transmission across the synaptic gap.

row.subject: Science
row.questionText: What happens at the synapse between two neurons?
row.answer: At the synapse, electrical impulses arriving at the axonal end of one neuron trigger the release of neurotransmitter chemicals. These diffuse across the synaptic gap and bind to receptors on the dendrite of the next neuron, generating a new electrical impulse.
solutionSteps: Impulse reaches pre-synaptic axonal end.
Neurotransmitters released into synaptic cleft.
They diffuse across the gap and bind to dendrite receptors of next neuron.
New impulse generated → signal continues.
row.finalAnswer: Electrical → chemical (neurotransmitter) → electrical signal transmission across synaptic gap.
